title: How to Solve Grade 3 Word Problems (A 7-Step Method That Works on Any Problem) + Free Quiz
meta_title: How to Solve Grade 3 Word Problems + Free Quiz
meta_desc: A repeatable 7-step method to solve grade 3 word problems on any question, with a clue-word chart, a free 8-question quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: Most Grade 3 children can add and multiply just fine — they freeze when the maths is hidden inside a story. Here is the one step-by-step method I teach that works on any word problem, plus a quick quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Aarav can rattle off his 6 times table and add three-digit numbers without blinking. Then his teacher writes ‘A kirana shop had 348 eggs and sold 176. How many are left?’ and he stops dead, pencil hovering, asking ‘do I plus or minus?’ If that sounds like your child, the good news is this: the arithmetic is not the problem. Knowing how to solve grade 3 word problems — how to pull the maths out of a story — is a separate skill, and it is one you can teach with a single repeatable method.

I have used the same seven steps with hundreds of eight-year-olds, from Tier 2 city classrooms to weekend tuition batches. It works because it slows the child down at exactly the two places they rush: understanding the story, and checking the answer. Here it is.

The 7 steps to solve any grade 3 word problem

Teach these in order. For the first week, say them out loud together; within a fortnight most children run through them silently.

  • Read it twice. Once for the story, once for the numbers. One read is never enough.
  • Underline the question. What is actually being asked? Answers ‘how many left’ and ‘how many altogether’ need very different maths.
  • Circle the numbers and the clue words. Find every number and the word that tells you what to do with it.
  • Decide the operation. Add, subtract, multiply or divide — and be ready to defend the choice.
  • Estimate first. Roughly, should the answer be bigger or smaller? About how big?
  • Solve it. Now, and only now, do the actual calculation.
  • Check it makes sense. Put the answer back into the story. Does 524 eggs left from a box of 348 sound right? No — so something went wrong.

How clue words map to operations

Clue words are signposts. When a child spots ‘altogether’ or ‘each’, it nudges them toward the right operation. Here is the chart I stick inside the back of every child’s maths copy.

Clue wordsUsually meansExample
altogether, sum, total, in all, combinedAddDiya read 34 pages, then 28 more. How many in all?
left, fewer, how many more, difference, remainSubtract250 mangoes, 90 sold. How many left?
each, per, groups of, rows of, timesMultiply6 boxes with 8 pencils each. How many pencils?
shared, split, equally, divided amongDivide₹60 shared equally among 5 friends. How much each?

The warning that matters most

Here is the honest caveat, and it is the one thing most clue-word charts leave out: clue words can lie. Take ‘Rohan has 12 marbles. He has 4 more than his sister. How many does she have?’ The word ‘more’ screams add — but the answer is 12 − 4 = 8. A child who blindly follows clue words gets it wrong every time.

So I teach clue words as a hint, never a rule. The real question is always: what is happening in the story? If the child can retell the problem in their own words, they will pick the right operation even when the clue word is trying to trick them. Understanding the story beats spotting a keyword. Every single time.

Estimating: the step everyone skips

Estimating before solving feels like extra work to a child, so they fight it. Insist anyway. If a problem asks how many left after selling 176 of 348 eggs, a quick estimate says ‘about 350 minus about 180, so roughly 170.’ When the child then works it out carefully and gets 172, they know it is right. And if they had accidentally added and got 524, the estimate would have caught it. Estimation is not a frill; it is the child’s own error alarm.

A worked example, start to finish

Let us run the full method on one problem: ‘A cricket coach buys 7 packets of balls. Each packet has 6 balls. He already had 15 balls. How many balls does he have now?’

  • Read twice — it is about a coach buying and adding up cricket balls.
  • Question — how many balls now (total).
  • Numbers and clues — 7 packets, 6 ‘each’ (multiply), 15 already had, ‘now’ total (add).
  • Operation — this is a two-step problem: multiply, then add.
  • Estimate — about 7 × 6 is roughly 42, plus 15, so around 55–60.
  • Solve — 7 × 6 = 42, then 42 + 15 = 57.
  • Check — 57 is close to our estimate of 55–60, and it is more than 15, which makes sense because he bought more. Correct.

Notice this problem needed two operations. Grade 3 introduces these two-step problems, and the seven-step method handles them without any change — you simply decide there are two operations at step four.

How much practice, and what kind

Fifteen minutes, three or four days a week, beats a marathon on Sunday. Mix the operations deliberately. When every problem on a page is subtraction, the child stops reading and just subtracts — the exact habit we are trying to break. A page with addition, subtraction, multiplication and division jumbled together forces them to actually think about each story. That mixed practice is where genuine confidence with how to solve grade 3 word problems is built.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free 8-question quiz built on this method — a mix of all four operations plus one that tries to trick you with clue words. Let your child work through it and read the explanations for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer graded practice, the printable mixed word-problems worksheet at the end gives plenty of jumbled questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 3 Word Problems Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight mixed word problems covering all four operations. Read each one twice, decide the operation, then pick your answer and press Check my score.

questions.q: Diya read 34 pages on Monday and 28 pages on Tuesday. How many pages did she read altogether?
A kirana shop had 250 mangoes and sold 90. How many are left?
There are 6 boxes and each box has 8 pencils. How many pencils in all?
₹60 is shared equally among 5 friends. How much does each friend get?
Rohan has 12 marbles. He has 4 more than his sister. How many does his sister have?
questions.explanation: This one tricks you. ‘More’ sounds like add, but the sister has fewer, so 12 − 4 = 8. Always check the story.

questions.q: A coach buys 7 packets of balls with 6 balls in each packet. How many balls did he buy?
A school had 348 students. 176 went on a trip. How many stayed back?
questions.explanation: ‘How many stayed back’ means subtract: 348 − 176 = 172 students.

questions.q: Aarav buys 4 pens at ₹9 each. He pays with a ₹50 note. How much change does he get?
questions.explanation: Two steps: 4 × 9 = 36 for the pens, then 50 − 36 = ₹14 change.

faq.q: Why does my child do sums fine but freeze on word problems?
faq.a: Because reading the maths out of a story is a different skill from the arithmetic itself. The calculation may be easy, but deciding which operation the story needs is the hard part — and that is exactly what the seven-step method trains.

faq.q: Are clue words like ‘altogether’ and ‘left’ reliable?
faq.a: They are helpful hints, not rules. Some problems use ‘more’ but need subtraction. Teach clue words as a first clue, then always check what is actually happening in the story before choosing the operation.

faq.q: What is a two-step word problem in Grade 3?
faq.a: One that needs two operations, such as multiply then add: ‘7 packets of 6 balls, plus 15 already owned.’ The same seven-step method handles it — you simply notice there are two operations when you decide what to do.

faq.q: How much word-problem practice does a Grade 3 child need?
faq.a: About fifteen minutes, three or four days a week, with the operations mixed up on the page. Jumbled practice forces the child to read and think about each problem instead of repeating one operation.
